opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I see it, the biggest bottleneck in robot learning right now isn't really the algorithms. It's the data. In vision and language, the field had the internet: billions of images and documents that already existed and just needed to be collected. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no giant archive of robots folding laundry or cooking dinner sitting around waiting for us. We have to create that data, and creating it is expensive, slow, and usually very fragmented.

Right now most labs collect their own small datasets on their own robots with their own setups. The data gets used for one paper and then basically sits on a hard drive. So a big part of what I hope to achieve by organizing research around a data platform is to change that dynamic, so that data becomes infrastructure rather than a byproduct.

Concretely, that means a few things. First, scaling up how we collect data. That includes making teleoperation and human demonstration much cheaper and more intuitive, and also tapping into sources like human videos or handheld devices, where you don't even need a robot in the loop. Second, making the data reusable across different robots, tasks, and environments, so a demonstration collected in one setting can still teach something useful somewhere else. Third, closing the loop: understanding which data actually matters. Not all demonstrations are equal. Some are much more informative than others, and if we can figure out data quality and data curation, we can get much more out of every hour of collection.

The bigger picture is that I think a platform-centered approach lets research compound. Instead of every project starting from scratch, each new model, each new collection effort, each new evaluation builds on a shared foundation. That's how I think we eventually get to robots that are generally capable in messy, real human environments, like homes and hospitals, rather than robots that only work in the one lab where they were trained.

r001.rationale: It describes organizing robotics research around a data platform so projects build on a shared foundation, rather than starting from scratch.

r002.rationale: It does not propose using researchers’ credibility to earn data vendors’ trust.

r003.rationale: It does not say robotics research can increase the credibility of vendor-supplied data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I think robotics has a data problem that's quite different from the one computer vision or NLP had, and I don't think we solve it by individual labs each collecting a few hundred demonstrations and training a model on their own.

When I look at how progress happened in vision and language, it wasn't just that someone built a better architecture. It was that the field converged on shared datasets and shared infrastructure, so that when one group had an idea, everyone else could test it against the same thing, and the data itself kept compounding. Robotics hasn't had that. Every lab has its own robot, its own teleop setup, its own data format, and the data mostly dies when the paper is published.

So when I say organizing research around a data platform, I mean a few things. One is making data collection a first-class engineering problem rather than an afterthought. Things like how you get demonstrations cheaply, how you make them diverse enough to actually matter, how you mix human teleop with simulation and autonomous rollouts. Second is standardization, so that data from different embodiments and different tasks can actually be pooled and learned from together. And third, and maybe most important to me, is that the platform should let you ask scientific questions about data. What kinds of demonstrations are actually useful? How much does diversity in scenes matter versus diversity in objects? When does more data stop helping? Right now those questions are mostly answered by anecdote, and I'd like them to be answered by experiments that other people can reproduce.

What I hope comes out of it is that a student with a good idea about learning algorithms doesn't need to spend eight months building a teleop rig before they can test it. And that the field starts to accumulate knowledge about data the way it has accumulated knowledge about models.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared datasets, infrastructure, and standardized data that researchers can pool and test against together as a way to organize robotics research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention using researchers’ credibility to earn data vendors’ trust.

r003.rationale: It does not state that robotics research can increase the credibility of vendor-supplied data.

astra-6.text:
The hope is to make the data we collect useful beyond a single robot or a single task. In robotics, we often build the whole pipeline for each project: collect data, train a model, evaluate it, and then start over for the next problem. A data platform could let those efforts build on one another.

And it’s more than storing a lot of demonstrations. We need to understand what the data covers, where our models fail, and what we should collect next. If we can connect those pieces, we can create a cycle where deploying and testing robots helps us gather better data, and that data helps us build more capable robots. Ultimately, I want researchers to spend less time rebuilding infrastructure and more time exploring how robots can learn and generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says a data platform could let robotics projects build on one another and make data useful across robots and tasks, communicating a shared basis for research collaboration.

r002.rationale: It does not mention researchers using their credibility to earn data vendors’ trust.

r003.rationale: It does not say robotics research can increase the credibility of vendor-supplied data.

sol-6.1.text:
The hope is to make it easier for people to build on each other’s work. In robotics, we often collect data for one robot or one task, train a model, and then repeat that process for the next problem. A shared data platform could help us connect those efforts, so that new data contributes to a broader capability instead of staying isolated in one project.

It’s also a way to organize the research questions: What data are we missing? Which experiences actually help a robot learn? How do we measure whether it can generalize to a new environment? Ultimately, I’d like the platform to support a cycle where robots collect useful experience, we learn from it, and those improvements help robots handle a wider range of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says a shared data platform can connect robotics efforts and make it easier for researchers to build on each other’s work.

r002.rationale: It does not propose using researchers’ credibility to earn data vendors’ trust.

r003.rationale: It does not say robotics research can increase the credibility of vendor-supplied data.
